questions.q: Who has nothing but mockery for Job?
questions.a: Those who are younger than Job have nothing but mockery for him.

questions.q: What made the young men’s fathers thin?
questions.a: They were thin from poverty and hunger.

questions.q: From where were the young men’s fathers driven out?
questions.a: Their fathers were driven out from among people.

questions.q: Of whom does Job say the young men’s fathers are descendants?
questions.a: Job says that they were descendants of fools, indeed, of worthless men.

questions.q: What had Job become for the sons of the worthless men?
questions.a: Job had become their subject for a song of mockery.

questions.q: What do the people now cast away in front of Job?
questions.a: These people cast away self-restraint in front of him.

questions.q: Why are the men able to advance his calamity for Job?
questions.a: They advance his calamity because there is no one to hold them back.

questions.q: What does Job say is driven away by the wind?
questions.a: His dignity is driven away as if by the wind.

questions.q: What has laid hold of Job as his life is pouring out within him?
questions.a: Many days of suffering have laid hold on him.

questions.q: What does Job say has changed his clothing?
questions.a: Skin disease has changed his skin, referred to as clothing.

questions.q: How does Job say God has changed?
questions.a: God has changed and become cruel to him; with the power of his hand God persecutes him.

questions.q: What does Job know is destined for all living things?
questions.a: He knows that God will bring him to death, to the house destined for all living things.

questions.q: What came when Job waited for light?
questions.a: When he waited for light, darkness came instead.

questions.q: Where did Job stand to call for help?
questions.a: He stood up in the assembly and cried for help.

questions.q: For what kind of music does Job say his harp is tuned?
questions.a: Job says that his harp is tuned for songs of mourning.

commentary.text: Job's honour is turned into contempt.

Verses 1–14 Job contrasts his present condition with his former honour and authority. What little cause have men to be ambitious or proud of that which may be so easily lost, and what little confidence is to be put in it! We should not be cast down if we are despised, reviled, and hated by wicked men. We should look to Jesus, who endured the contradiction of sinners.

Job complains a great deal. Harbouring hard thoughts of God was the sin which did, at this time, most easily beset Job. When inward temptations join with outward calamities, the soul is hurried as in a tempest, and is filled with confusion. But woe be to those who really have God for an enemy! Compared with the awful state of ungodly men, what are all outward, or even inward temporal afflictions? There is something with which Job comforts himself, yet it is but a little. He foresees that death will be the end of all his troubles. God's wrath might bring him to death; but his soul would be safe and happy in the world of spirits. If none pity us, yet our God, who corrects, pities us, even as a father pitieth his own children. And let us look more to the things of eternity: then the believer will cease from mourning, and joyfully praise redeeming love.
